raw_response.country: United Kingdom (Scotland, with comparative discussion of England)

criterion_notes.c1: Does not examine household or community water or sanitation service access; instead discusses high-level economic regulation and customer representation in negotiating Scottish Water's business plan, explicitly noting that unserved populations were not considered in the Forum's work or the business plan.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: YES — examines legal, regulatory, and governance arrangements in water utility regulation (Scottish Water's public corporation model, WICS price-setting powers under the Water Industry (Scotland) Act 2002 and Water Services (Scotland) Act 2005, and the Customer Forum). Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: NO — focuses on participatory stakeholder negotiation of a utility business plan and reducing regulatory burden rather than analysing how a rule-type mechanism (such as tariff rules, eligibility screening, tenure/documentation, or utility ownership/regulatory structure) directly governs household or community service access. Even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the paper is excluded (plain_criterion2_decision = exclude) because it contains no empirical evidence (c3) and reports no service-access outcome (c4).
criterion_notes.c3: Non-empirical legal/policy commentary and first-person experiential reflection by a member of the Customer Forum, with no empirical research design, primary data collection, or systematic empirical synthesis. Excluded under E05.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports no empirical outcome measuring household or community water/sanitation access, connection, availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion; only describes reaching a negotiated agreement on Scottish Water's draft business plan ahead of schedule.
criterion_notes.c5: Lacks an empirical study design, defined study population/sample, and measurable service-access outcome.

evidence_quotes.quote: This article will explore recent initiatives in customer engagement in water services in Scotland, UK.
including, perhaps, those who are not served by Scottish Water and therefore not really considered in our work or the business plan
Influenced by these developments in England, and the emerging literature, it was agreed to establish a body known as the Customer Forum in Scotland.
The paper’s author was a member of the Forum and will therefore be able to combine academic analysis with an experiential understanding of the process.
With this support and regulatory commitment, it was possible for the Forum’s engagement committee to reach agreement with Scottish Water on a draft business plan

raw_response.exposure: Customer Forum negotiated-settlement mechanism within the Water Industry Commission for Scotland (WICS) 2015 strategic review of charges
raw_response.outcome: Agreement between the Customer Forum and Scottish Water on a draft business plan (no household or community water or sanitation access outcome reported)
raw_response.rationale: Full text matches metadata (Hendry 2016, Water Policy, DOI 10.2166/wp.2016.199). Excluded as E05 (No empirical evidence): the article is a legal/regulatory policy essay and first-person institutional reflection by an academic member of Scotland's Customer Forum describing how the Forum negotiated a draft business plan with Scottish Water under WICS oversight, with comparative discussion of England's Customer Challenge Groups. It has no empirical methodology, sample, or primary data analysis, and it does not examine household or community water/sanitation access outcomes (explicitly noting on p. 12 that unserved populations were not considered in the Forum's work). It would also be excluded under the plain wording of Criterion 2 for lack of empirical evidence and lack of any access outcome.
